subtopic: EFFECT OF CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
EFFECT OF CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what is the price we will have to pay for the so-called free trade agreement? It could be staggering. First there will be job losses. No one knows the exact number but some estimates run as high as 500,000 jobs, as indicated by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) himself. We will then lose our ability to shape our own economy and to develop our own economic, social and environmental policies.
In the case of energy, we give the United States guaranteed access to our resources without getting guaranteed access to U.S. resources. Furthermore, we will give away the power to set our own prices for our own energy. Our own decision making powers in energy matters will be seriously diminished. Of course, these conclusions are based on the information available so far. Believe it or not, Mr. Speaker, we have not yet seen the final text of the trade agreement.
There is, of course, an alternative. We could liberalize trade between provinces and liberalize trade internationally, not just in North America. We are better suited for an international trade policy. We must reverse the decline in Canadian trade with other parts of the world. What we want first and foremost is not to give away our ability to determine the future we want for this and future generations of Canadians.

subsubtopic: OFFICIAL OPENING OF CANADIAN INSTITUTE OF INDUSTRIAL TECHNOLOGY IN WINNIPEG
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle)
and I officially opened the Canadian Institute of Industrial Technology in Winnipeg-a world-class show piece-federal Government, universities, and the private sector working together-a new era of computer integrated manufacturing and industrial technology.
Almost since its inception, nattering nabobs of negativism have been hounding the institute. First they predicted the $26 million project would be cancelled. When that did not happen they predicted the Government would build it and then sell it. When the centre was completed and open for business in early 1986, the critics began describing it as a white elephant, then as an empty or half empty building.
Well, Mr. Speaker, last week a miracle occurred. Critics finally got the message that 40 per cent empty is 60 per cent full. In a year, organizations will be on a waiting list to grab up the little remaining space. Nattering nabobs of negativism, go to your graves!

subsubtopic: PROPOSED SALE OF CN TOWER
speechtext:
Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, the Government of Egypt selling off the Pyramids, the Chinese people placing the Great Wall on the auction block, or the Eiffel Tower turned over to the private sector? Only in Canada we say "sell the CN Tower"! And what is the CN Tower to be called; Alpo Dog Food Heights, Loblaws Skyscraper, Pizza Pizza Peak or perhaps Ronald Reagan Lookout?
I find it astounding that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) measures the value of a structure by whether or not it can go choo-choo-chooing along. The CN Tower doesn't do that, but then, again, it's never late.
The Tower was built with $57 million of Canadian money. It does serve 15 media centres. It does accommodate two million visitors a year, and it does bring a sense of pride to Canadians. All of this, and the Tower turned a tidy $5 million profit last year.
If the Government insists on bequeathing the CN Tower to the private sector, it should at least attempt to secure a guarantee that the purchaser will find a small place for the Government's epitaph to be displayed for all Canadians to see.

December 2, 1987

subsubtopic: PASSAGE OF LEGISLATION URGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to support Bill C-54, an Act to control pornography in Canada. I urge all Members of this House to pass it as quickly as possible and send the legislation to committee.
Not a week goes by that someone from my riding of Niagara Falls does not write to me to urge quick passage of this legislation. They know that the present provisions governing pornography in the Criminal Code are so vague as to be almost unenforceable. Pornography has become a gigantic industry, one that exploits and degrades people, particularly women and children.
I reject comments from groups who say that the definition of pornography is too restrictive. I challenge them to appear before our committee and suggest a better definition. I believe that is only fair.
In the meantime, people everywhere are getting tired of those individuals who continuously want to postpone a crackdown on pornography. As it relates to this piece of legislation I am determined that that will not happen.

subsubtopic: MONTREAL EAST END-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after fifteen months the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and Minister of State for Science and Technology has decided to respond to the Picard Report's eighty-six recommendations this morning in Montreal. The people of Montreal were expecting concrete proposals but unfortunately, the Minister's response was just a lot of bluffing. I would like to know, and so would the people of Montreal, why the Minister failed to announce the establishment of a space agency in Montreal. Why didn't the Minister announce that a real banking centre would be set up in Montreal? Why didn't the Minister announce that $130 million would be provided to fund development of the Old Port in Montreal, as was done in the case of other Canadian cities? Why didn't the Minister announce that $25 million would be made available to the Montreal East development board? Expansion failed to provide the people of Montreal with anything tangible.

subsubtopic: NATIONAL COUNCIL OF WELFARE-SUGGESTED COMMITTEE STUDY OF REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the just published report of the National Council of Welfare which provides advice to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) is appropriately entitled "Welfare in Canada-The Tangled Safety Net".
It points out that the current social assistance system, although it has some good points, very often reinforces poverty and engenders continued dependence upon welfare. People can get caught in the net rather than being saved by it. The report addresses issues such as simplification, accessibility, equity, adequacy, and due process.
The House of Commons Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare ought to make a thorough study of the report to see which of its recommendations might successfully be implemented.

subsubtopic: WINE INDUSTRY-ELECTION PROMISE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) of the pledge he made to the grape growers of the Niagara Peninsula when he was campaigning during the 1984 election campaign.
During that campaign the Prime Minister vowed to 'revitalize the industry and keep our farmers farming". He said that the wine industry was "in a state of crisis caused in great part by the unfair trade practices of offshore wine producers". Then he vowed that a Conservative Government would promote Canadian wines and related products and adopt other protective measures because that would be "far less costly to the public treasury than to allow this vital Niagara industry to literally wither on the vine".
If the free trade deal goes through, the wine industry will wither on the vine. The Prime Minister who promised to protect the industry, who had a clear mandate to protect it, has instead betrayed it.
December 2, 1987

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: EFFECT OF AGREEMENT ON AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, members of the Union des producteurs agricoles are having a convention in Quebec City.
Since the president, Jacques Proulx, will take advantage of this opportunity to continue his disinformation campaign, I would like to inform the Elouse of the positive impact our free trade agreement wil have on agriculture. This Government has earmarked $1.5 billion for the dairy industry over the next five years. Subsidy policies will continue to apply to farm producers, whatever their president may say to the contrary. Our subsidy policies and quota systems which are so important for farmers will continue to apply. Our marketing boards will not be effected by the free trade agreement.
I may add that our major processors have not spoken out against free trade, that Lactantia, a company that buys 40 per cent of Quebec's milk production, is in favour of free trade, and that agricultural by-products such as beef will find additional markets in United States.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, if farm producers have any business sense at all, they should not protest against free trade. They should challenge their president, Mr. Jacques Proulx!

subsubtopic: ROUTE CANADA-CLOSURE OF OPERATIONS IN SYDNEY, N.S.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Route Canada, formerly CN Route, formerly CN Express, closed its operations in Sydney. The federal Government sold what is now Route Canada for less than its value on the understanding that all the closing of the terminals would be done by the new owner, thereby sparing the federal Government from giving the bad news.
Route Canada, the federal Government, and the union took away protection the workers had under the Canada Labour Code. The men in Sydney were dismissed with only two weeks' notice, and the 17 dismissed in Sydney had a range of service between 16 and 46 years. Route Canada has made it look like it just dismissed the individuals when, in fact, it closed the terminal.
The federal Government offered benefits to those workers if they resigned prior to June 1, 1987. But the workers in Sydney were dismissed only five months later, which shows that there was collusion between the federal Government and the
company because the workers only received a fraction of the federal benefits that the company had to give.
I ask the federal Government to extend the benefit package which expired on June 1, 1987, to the workers who were just dismissed at CN Route.

subsubtopic: SUPPORT FOR NEW CANADIAN MULTICULTURALISM ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the introduction in the House yesterday of the proposed Multicultural Act was a milestone in Canadian history.
Wrapped up in the word "multiculturalism" are many different concepts. Of course it means the right to retain one's culture, heritage, and language. But it also includes the concept of getting to know and understand each other better, the concept of equal opportunity for all, and the concept of full involvement and participation in wider Canadian society. It means that you can be proud of your background and that of your ancestors, and at the same time be fiercely proud to be a Canadian.
Multiculturalism is a Canadian creation. It has helped us to achieve stability and social harmony in spite of our great diversity. In doing so, it is the envy of the world.
Multiculturalism is a vital part of what makes Canadians different, a vital part of our Canadian way of life, a vital part of our national sovereignty. The Multiculturalism Act will help to reinforce and strengthen our national sovereignty.

subsubtopic: THE ECONOMIST'S REPORT ON CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the current issue of The Economist, perhaps the most respected financial journal in the world, has bad news for the Liberals and their socialist partners in the House. The Economist has given Canada a glowing report card.
The Economist states that "Canada's producers are thriving". Those are its words. "Our output", it says, "is up 6.1 per cent to August this year", better than any other country it reviews. That 6.1 per cent for Canada compares with slightly more than 4 per cent for the United States and Japan, a negative return for West Germany, and less than 2 per cent and 3 per cent for France and Great Britain.
The figures show without a doubt that our Government is on the right economic course, that indeed our policies are working and are good for Canada, and that they are certainly good for Ontario. Freer trade with the United States will make it even better.
I invite Hon. Members to read The Economist for this week and to take a look at page 107 for themselves.

subsubtopic: SCHEDULED RELEASE OF PARKER COMMISSION REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House of Commons and the country have been waiting patiently for a long time for the Parker Commission Report into allegations of conflict of interest against the former Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion.
The Government has had the final copy for several days, and I understand that it has announced today that it will be made public tomorrow at three o'clock.

The Government has claimed to introduce civility into the House of Commons. Failure to give advance copies, as is the usual rule, will be a demonstration of hypocrisy on the part of the Government. I hope that it will give the usual advance copies.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT SIGNING OF AGREEMENT BE DELAYED FOR TWO MONTHS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I indicated to the Leader of the Opposition, the parties are now putting into a legal, final version the elements of the agreement that were tabled in this House early in October.
Of course, we are also discussing implementation procedures. That is a highly technical, very complex document that requires a tremendous amount of attention and care from the negotiators.
Of course, as in any negotiations or discussions of this kind, either party may raise a question, and the other of course has an obligation to listen.

subsubtopic: AIRPORTS-TRANSFER OF BAGGAGE FROM DOMESTIC TO INTERNATIONAL FLIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. Yesterday the Minister of Transport said there were two exceptions to a passenger match when baggage is put on board aircraft. Today we learn from people involved in baggage transfers of another exception. When baggage is transferred to a connecting international flight from a domestic flight it is not x-rayed or verified so as to ensure complete security. subsubtopic: PEACEKEEPING IN CENTRAL AMERICA-STATEMENT BY SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to report to the House upon my conversations and meetings last week in Nicaragua, Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras and Costa Rice and, in particular, to discuss the peace process agreed to unanimously by the five

December 2, 1987
Statements by Ministers
Central American Presidents in their August meeting at Esquipulas.
That agreement seeks to achieve "the climate of liberty that democracy ensures", and it sets forth conditions with which all five Governments must comply. Two characteristics invest this agreement with unusual promise. It is unanimous and it is indigenous. It is not a prescription from outside but a commitment made deliberately by all five Presidents.
It is my impression, after talking to each President, that all intend to keep the word they gave. Indeed, a strength of this agreement is that no one-no Government, no guerilla force, no outside power-will want to stand accused of making this agreement fail. It is, therefore, of unusual importance that, in addition to whatever help countries like Canada might offer, we seek to create a public opinion that is informed and dispassionate about this process so that compliance can be fairly judged and pressure for compliance fully maintained.
No peace is simple. Countries which are serious about contributing to the success of this process must begin by understanding the complexity of the conflicts and the history of Central America and understanding also the relative frailty of the democracy which this accord seeks to promote.
Only eight years ago, in 1979, Costa Rica was the only democracy in the region. The Government of Nicaragua then was an oppressive, almost feudal, regime, a regime which invited revolution. The tradition in the region, again excepting Costa Rica, has been for crises to be resolved by force and military rule. There are, therefore, no deep roots for the democratic parties and institutions which can guarantee civil liberties and human rights as we Canadians have come to understand them.
The region is still torn by extremism-extremism of the right, extremism of the left-and it is marked by poverty, injustice and exploitation. Its economy is hobbled by debt, low commodity prices, frequent inefficiency, and the spectre and reality of war which drive growth away and distort domestic priorities. Even nature has been cruel. The capital cities of Managua, Guatemala and San Salvador have all been struck visibly by earthquakes. Those, Sir, are the circumstances in which the five Presidents seek peace.
Moreover, despite their unanimity, there are deep suspicions among them-doubts that the civil authorities in El Salvador, Guatemala and, to a lesser degree, Honduras, will in the end be strong enough to control the army, to control the police, to end the tradition of repression. There is also a profound skepticism as to whether the Sandinistas will let real democracy threaten the revolution which their constitution describes as irreversible.
In addition, each Government which signed the agreement must deal with combatants and refugees who have not been parties to this accord and whose views only become known in piecemeal fashion. That is to mention simply the complexities of the region itself which are complicated further by the
extension to Central America of the competition between the United States and the Soviet Union.
There are, Sir, plenty of obstacles, but there is also a genuine commitment to the peace initiative and a recognition that the alternative is hopeless; continued bloodshed, economic stagnation, the withering of young, democratic institutions, and the consequent rebirth of coercive forces of the right and of the left.

Canada's interest and involvement in Central America is relatively recent, but our standing is high. Over the last five years we have tripled our bilateral aid to over $105 million, and, on a per capita basis, our aid to Central America is second only to what we do in the Caribbean. In that period, total direct Canadian assistance amounted to nearly $170 million, including support for Canadian non-governmental organizations who are active throughout the region.
To get some better sense of the people and, the countryside, we visited a Farmers For Peace workshop in Nicaragua where farmers are trained to repair machinery.
We visited also two NGO projects in southern Honduras, one where Horizons For Friendship helps educate orphans, and the other, a rural clinic operated by Canadian church workers.
Members of our delegation visited different CIDA projects-with purposes ranging from purifying water to providing daycare for single parents, to improving dairy production, to building houses, and meeting other practical needs.
Some of our delegation also met with human rights groups, womens' associations, artists, and refugees in the camp at Limon. We saw for ourselves the good reputation of Canada, which gives us credentials to contribute to the peace process.
The Accord asks "the respect and support of the international community for our efforts. We have plans in Central America for peace and development, but we need help to make them a reality."
I had planned to visit the region sometime before the Spring of next year to provide a visible signal of Canada's support. I sought to meet, in seven days, as broad as possible a representation of the people and organizations who, because they are involved in the conflict, must be brought into the process of peace. I had meetings with the five Presidents; the five Foreign Ministers; other Ministers and commandantes; the two clerics, Cardinal Obando y Bravo and Archbishop Rivera y Damas who are charged with leading reconciliation in, respectively, Nicaragua and El Salvador; leaders of the political wing of the guerrillas in El Salvador; a contra representative in Costa Rica, Alfredo Cesar, who was once the head of the Nicaraguan Central Bank under the Sandinistas; the Miskito Indian Leader Brooklyn Rivera; Opposition leaders in Nicaragua including Pablo Antonio Cuadra, the noted poet and co-
December 2, 1987

director of La Prensa, and groups preoccupied with human rights.
In addition, our delegation included Lieutenant-Colonel Don Ethell and Lieutenant Colonel Gerald Thompson, two Canadian officers who have commanded international peacekeeping operations elsewhere in the world. They had detailed discussions with Central American authorities about the practical challenges of designing and operating verification and peacekeeping mechanisms.
I have just laid upon the Table of the House the basic document that was used by those two representatives of our military in their discussions in Central America.
The Esquipulas plan proposes procedures of verification and follow-up, but I told each President of Canada's concern that they were underestimating the complexity of putting such mechanisms in place. A peacekeeping operation must fit precisely the conditions in the regions where the peace is to be kept. You cannot simply shift a model that might work in Cyprus to the very different conditions of Central America.
Our experts believe that it could take up to six months to design and mount a mechanism that would prove effective in Central America. I said that Canadian expertise would be available for all or part of that work, if the five Presidents agreed unanimously that they wanted Canadian help. I emphasized, Sir, that we were not seeking an invitation, because we want the decision on this vital question to be taken by Central America for Central American reasons. I indicated that there were general conditions of unanimity and authority that Canada requires before becoming involved in any aspect of any peacekeeping operations.
I should tell the House that I do not think it would be appropriate to attach new conditions in this case, since the problems in Central America are already complex enough. As a result of our conversations, I believe the five Governments now have a greater sense of the urgency of getting on with the design of the mechanisms that they will need.
Peace and the peace plan are the overwhelming preoccupation in Central America now. Naturally, other issues arise. Let me deal with two of them, the question of the conditionality of aid, and the resumption of our program in Guatemala.
There has been a suggestion that, in the special circumstances of Central America, Canada should abandon the principle of not using our aid for political purposes. Part of the reason that Canada is respected in the world is precisely because our aid has been designed to help the poorest, to help the most needy. Other countries, including the United States, use aid for political leverage, and their reputation reflects their practice just as our reputation reflects our practice. If we make an exception in Central America, we would begin to discount that distinctive, valuable Canadian principle.
Statements by Ministers
I discussed the question in Central America, including with President Arias, who understands and accepts Canada's policy. I make the point, Sir, that it would be consistent with our practice to consider help to special multilateral mechanisms which the five Presidents might jointly establish to promote democratization or compliance or other specific purposes in the region as a whole and as part of the evolution of the peace process.
[ Translation]
We are maintaining active development projects in Nicaragua, Honduras, Costa Rica, and El Salvador, and have announced our intention to resume bilateral aid to Guatemala. We will follow in Guatemala the precedent established two years ago in El Salvador, which allows control of our aid to rest in Canadian hands, at least until the program is well launched. That system has proven very effective in El Salvador. Some critics in Canada believe Guatemala should continue to be left out of bilateral programs, because of their human rights record. Unquestionably, abuses of human rights continue. The questions are first whether the democratically-elected government of President Cerezo has made enough progress on human rights to justify resumption of aid and second whether it is now safe for Canadian aid workers to deliver that program. The Gatemalan Human Rights Commission in exile, the Inter-American Human Rights Commission of the OAS, the U.N. Special Representative for Guatemala, and Amnesty International have all noted signs of improvement in Guatemala under the civilian government while indicating, as we would agree, that abuses continue. My judgment is that there has been progress, and that bilateral aid relation with Canada will encourage further progress on human rights in Guatemala.

Obviously, another question in Canada concerns the public position we should take regarding the support by the United States of the Contras, and the support by the Soviet Union and Cuba of the Sandinista Government and of guerrilla activity in El Salvador. We oppose third party intervention in Central America, whatever the source, and have made that position clear to both superpowers.
Some Canadians argue sincerely that our Central American policy should focus more on public criticism of the United States. I believe that such a policy would reduce, and not increase, whatever real influence we might have in Washington on this question. It could, in addition, impede our ability to play other, more active roles in support of the peace plan. The five Governments of Central America are in no doubt about the difference between Canadian and U.S. policy, and our conduct should be guided by what makes us most effective in Central America itself.
The issue of compliance with the peace plan is most acute in three countries-Nicaragua, El Salvador, and Honduras.

December 2, 1987
Statements by Ministers
In Nicaragua, real commitments have been made to democratic reform-the formation of a National Reconciliation Commission, the reopening of La Prensa and Radio Catolica, the readmission of exiled clerics, and the release of almost 1,000 political prisoners. Earlier this month the Government also expressed a willingness to enter into indirect dialogue with the Contras, through the mediation of Cardinal Obando y Bravo. These commitments are real and they are encouraging. However, we should recall that by some estimates there are still between 7,000 and 8,000 political prisoners held in Nicaraguan jails, that some clerics remain in exile, that Radio Catolica was prevented from broadcasting its first newscast, and that the dialogue with the Contras is narrowly defined and still in very preliminary stages. There has been no complete amnesty.
In El Salvador, a full amnesty has been granted for political prisoners. Two prominent leaders of the political wing of the guerrilla movement have already taken advantage of this opening to return to that country's legitimate political process. The Salvadoran Government has also formed a National Reconciliation Commission and was quick to reopen talks with the guerrilla opposition. As well, El Salvador accepted the repatriation of some 4,300 Salvadoran refugees from camps inside Honduras. However, the violence continues in that country, and the Government-guerrilla dialogue was suspended after the assassination of Herbert Anaya, the head of the nongovernmental Human Rights Commission. Unfortunately, neither side seems prepared to take the serious initiatives needed to resume the dialogue.
Honduras is a country which does not have an internal conflict but is plagued with the problems of the Contra presence in the south, as well as the influx of enormous numbers of refugees from both Nicaragua and El Salvador. The Government has formed a National Reconciliation Commission to help deal with these problems. On the refugee side, as I noted, the Government co-operated fully with the UNHCR in the recent repatriation of Salvadoran refugees from Honduran camps. They have also asked the Contras to leave Honduran soil, though to date there has been no measurable movement. I was advised in Honduras that informal discussions may begin soon between Honduras and Nicaragua to move toward concrete compliance with the Esquipulas agreement respecting non-use of territory.
I remind the House that the notion of simultaneity, so central to this accord, means that implementation of the basic provisions of the accord must occur in lock-step. The Contras must be removed from Honduras at the same time as a ceasefire is negotiated between the Nicaraguan Government and the Contras. Neither objective has yet been reached, and each relies on the other.
I expressed at the outset my view of the importance of creating an active, informed, and dispassionate Canadian public opinion, whose interest and judgment might encourage compliance with the peace plan. I think it appropriate that the House of Commons pursue more formally the interest several
individual Members have already shown in the region and the process.
At the Government's request, House Leaders have begun discussions on the appropriate parliamentary committee to allow this House to monitor and encourage the peace process in Central America. I would place before that committee, on a monthly basis, a report on the current compliance with the plan and would seek to arrange other briefings and background. It might be useful for the committee to review the discussion paper on peacekeeping, which was just tabled and was the basis of our conversations last week, and to examine other ways by which Canada can contribute constructively to achieving peace. Officials of External Affairs, CIDA, and other Departments would be available to provide information.
Those of us who criticize the superpowers' involvement in Central America often unconsciously commit the error we condemn and see the region not by its own lights but in the shadow of a superpower. The initiative of the five Presidents is more than an attempt to resolve their own problems. It is an assertion of their distinct destiny. These are five countries with histories, aspirations, and identities of their own. Their development has been blunted by repression, poverty and conflict. Trade and tourists shift away from a region known as a war zone. Economic strategies are displaced by military strategies. Children, who should be in families, are orphaned. Youngsters, who should be in school, are at war.
The real issue in Central America is not Marxism, nor is it death squads, nor even is it the abuse of human rights. Those are symptoms. The root problems are economic and social, and Central America needs peace to resolve them.
Five different Presidents, with courage and uncommon unanimity, have launched their own initiative for peace. The issue now is whether the five Presidents who signed the accord will respect its principles, will keep moving toward peace, and will keep moving toward what they call in their own document "the climate of liberty that democracy ensures". I believe the House would agree that Canada should encourage and help them.

In one sense I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs falls short of the mark when he says that the problems are basically economic and social. Those may be the consequences, but I believe the problem has been the sense of imperialism, colonialism, or domination under which they have suffered. They have not lived in a world where there is a rule of law or where there is a recognition of the sovereign right of those countries to decide for themselves their own destiny, what kind of government they want to have, or what kind of economic and social systems they want to create. They have been dominated, manipulated, and pushed around. That is a cause that has inspired various countries and regions, not just for generations but for thousands of years. This is why I think that the opportunity for Canada to associate itself and to ally itself with that incredible historic initiative is something all Canadians support.
There is an understanding out there in the country. The Minister talks about trying to develop Canadian public opinion. It is there. It is amazing the number of churches and groups across the country that have sent people into Central America. It is amazing the number of people who have worked in co-ops in Nicaragua or Honduras and have direct experience from working in the most basic conditions. Canadians understand and recognize that they have a certain affinity for a small country trying to retain its independence in the looming shadow of a great power. That is why I looked forward to the Minister's visit. I really believe that when Canadians ask the question where we can play a role, here is a place for Canadian interest, Canadian affinity and a Canadian opportunity to do something meaningful, not by imposing our will but by providing many of those countries with the skills and support they are so desperately looking for.
One of the conversations in Nicaragua that I recall quite graphically was with one of the secondary Ministers. He told me that they were accused of being allied with the Soviets. What could they do, he said, when the Americans turned them down, started supporting the Contras and put an economic embargo on? Who did they have to turn to? Where else could they get support? It was only the Soviets and their bloc, he told me, who were prepared to come forward with the oil and sufficient economic aid to keep them alive. The Minister said, "Please, when you go back, tell your Government and country that we do not want to be associated with the Soviet Union. We want to be independent, but we need countries like Canada and others like you to give us that kind of support".
I have to express some disappointment with the Minister's remarks. I do not question or quarrel with his emotional sentiment. I think that he has been bitten, in a sense, by the same bug we all have when we go to Central America and we see the kind of struggle with which we all identify. But the Minister went there without a Central American policy and he
Statements by Ministers
has come back without one. We still do not have a policy as to how Canada will organize its various economic, diplomatic and political initiatives to meet the historic significance and the historic challenge that greets us in that region of the world.
Where I perhaps take quarrel the most, and I do it in all good intentions, is on the assertion the Minister makes that Canada should not speak out against U.S. aid to the Contras. That is the central issue in Central America. If the peace plan will work, aid to the Contras must stop. There is no other issue. All the rest of it is prelude and prologue. That is the central issue. Until that incredible, disruptive and immoral action comes to a halt, there will not be a peace plan. I believe sincerely, and I say it to the Minister, that Canada could play an important role in helping that aid to be halted.
When we visited Washington after our trip to Central America, the group that I was with met with a number of Congressman to talk about what would happen if Canada said no to Contra aid, specifically, clearly, directly, not in vague language of third party intervention, but clearly. They said that right now the issue is in the balance, that Congress must decide within a matter of months one way or the other. It is not the Reagan administration that will decide. Ultimately, it will be the Congress of the United States that will decide. There are people in that Congress fighting desperately to stop that aid on both sides of the House in both Parties. They said that if a country like Canada, with the kind of legitimacy and credibility that we have, seen as a good ally of the U.S., were to take the stand that the peace process is paramount and that the stoppage of aid is the priority, then that message would be heard in the halls of Congress. It might change 10 or 15 votes. I do not know the numbers, but they said it would have an impact and it would make a difference. We would add credibility.
Charges often heard in that kind of political debate about those going against aid to the Contras being soft on communism or something, the kind of rhetoric you hear from the right wing in the U.S., could be stopped if allies like Canada, the European countries and others took a stand. The American Congressmen told me that if we took a stand, then maybe some of the Europeans would take a stand, and all of a sudden the Americans would see it as the international community saying, "Stop this immoral practice". We could make a difference, Mr. Speaker. This Government could make a difference by saying in a forthright way, not in anger, not with vitriol, but by saying that if the peace process is to work you cannot have a surrogate war being sponsored by a great power which is designed to upset and overturn one of the partners to that peace process. That is what it is all about.
If I might be allowed a moment of anecdote, let me say this. Mr. Reagan does not know what he is doing. I believe he has no idea of the kind of inspiration that is in the hearts of many of those people in Nicaragua. I visited a farm village that had been attacked by the Contras five days earlier. As I walked into the village and watched the farmers and their families with rifles on their backs, I saw the destruction, the burned

December 2, 1987
Statements by Ministers
tractors, huts and granaries, and a little girl about seven years old approached. The translator told me that she wanted to show me her prize possession. It was a reading exercise book. She was the first one in her family to learn to read. That is what the revolution is about. As the Minister said, it is about children learning to read and proper health care. Her father said to me-I will never forget his words as he stood there- "You go back and tell Mr. Reagan that if he thinks he is going to take this away from me and my daughter, I will fight to the death to stop him". That is what is going on in that region. That is why it is so central for Canada to make its voice heard in a way that 1 think will ring not only through the Congress but throughout the corridors of Government in all parts of the world.
I realize there are dangers. I do not diminish the sense of caution of the Secretary of State for External Affairs', but if I may, through you, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say to the Secretary of State for External Affairs that this is a rare chance for a Canadian voice to be expressed in a way that would make a difference. I hope that this statement will not be the last word in our Central American policy. I hope, before the timetable of the peace process comes to an end, that we will say to our allies in the United States, "Stop aid".
In the next few minutes I would like to go beyond that. We should also tell the Americans to stop the economic embargo. This is something which the Minister did not mention in his statement. He spoke about poverty, economic difficulties and injustices. How would you like to be a country in which the largest power in the world is using its diplomatic influence to stop all trade, Mr. Speaker? Farmers for Peace, the Canadian aid project, send tools from Alberta, but they have to ship them to Costa Rica up a very difficult highway into Nicaragua. Inflation is 1000 per cent. When I arrived in Nicaragua, it was 55,000 cordobas to the dollar. When I left, it was 60,000 cordobas to the dollar. How can there be any kind of stability in that circumstance? The economic embargo is a large cause of that. We could be speaking out on that issue as well. If the process will work, you have to allow these countries to have some input into economic exchange. This is a Government that is talking about free trade, yet we are condoning a total blockage of trade of one of the countries in Central America.

speechtext:
I do not know whether the Parliamentary Secretary is being facetious, but I am trying to make a point and I wish he would take it seriously.
In this question of the use of economic aid-I think this is a special circumstance because of the peace process-we will have to be careful. If we do business as usual and offer an extra S14 million in aid to Honduras when it is still harbouring Contras, does that signal to some of the other countries that we are implicitly supporting that practice? In the discussions which the Secretary of State for External Affairs had with the President and the Foreign Minister of Honduras that subject should have been raised. We are the second largest donor in Honduras. We have clout and leverage. Our economic aid is not being given in a heavy-handed manner. The Americans, as the Minister probably recognizes, are tramping in and using their military aid as a way of trying to stop Honduras from making a change in its policy. The Reagan administration is clearly using its economic and military aid in Honduras to try to disrupt the peace plan. We should provide an alternative to that by saying that our country and others believe that, with the right gestures, we can do more.
In this case, I endorse fully what I believe was a commitment from the Minister. I do not want to put words in his mouth, but I do endorse the idea that there should be a Central American reconstruction plan and that Canada should take the lead in helping to pull that together. That is very important in allowing the other Central American countries, especially Honduras and El Salvador which are very dependent upon American aid, to know that if the peace plan succeeds and military aid is withdrawn, the economic vacuum will be filled.
One of the fears of those countries is that since American aid is such a dominant part of their economy, if it is pulled out, there will be nothing left. There must be a substantial contribution made by other countries of the world to fill that vacuum. I would hope that we could even go beyond that. I would hope that that would be an issue which the standing committee would address as well. It should address the question of whether or not Canada should take leadership by helping to organize, through the United Nations, NATO, the OECD and the various other multilateral groups to which we belong, a substantial reconstruction plan for Central America in order to provide a foundation for the peace plan.
A gesture that Canada could make immediately, even tomorrow, is to provide direct aid, perhaps through the auspices of the Red Cross, to help those countries carry out the amnesty. That costs money. If Contra rebels are to be persuaded to come from the hills back into the villages, they will need houses, training and farm tools. Those countries cannot afford that.
December 2, 1987

When I was there, members of the Nicaraguan Assembly asked us if we could find $50,000 in Canada to help them print their Constitution. They have no money with which to do that kind of work. An amount of $1 million in aid, an amount that is very small in terms of the CIDA budget, to help the resettlement of rebels and Contras, would have an enormous and magnifying impact on those countries. The money would not have to be given to the Governments. The Red Cross is already carrying out those kinds of functions, and aid targeted specifically at this early phase of the peace process would be a salutary and beneficial move.
I am not trying to fight the Minister's policy but I am saying that there are many elements that could go into that policy. There are elements of it that we could be implementing right now. This is not a condemnation of what the Minister saw and reported on, I am simply saying that there is a lot more that could be done.
Although my time is almost up, there is much more that I would like to say. I appreciate the fact that the Government will be establishing a committee, but in order to make that committee's work meaningful, the Government should place before it a clear statement of policy initiatives which we will be prepared to follow. Let the committee then debate and agonize over the issues and come to grips with them in a very quick and effective way. This should be done within a week or two, and my last message is that there is no time to waste.
The process is moving along. In some ways it is evolving, in some ways it is unravelling. Because the process is so crucial and historic and because there is an opportunity for Canadians to play a positive, beneficial and constructive role in it, we must take action immediately. We cannot wait for spring. That is why I urge the Minister to come forward with a policy, set up the committee and take the initiative.
I now return to my central point. Most important of all, we must be prepared to say clearly and without equivocation to our allies, using our influence, that after a proper assessment and judgment, the Government of Canada, with the support of the Canadian people, with members of the Opposition fully in accord, believes that the most important contribution Canada and the United States could make to peace in this world, to resolving the conflicts, would be to make a decision as quickly as possible that we will no longer support aid to that surrogate war that is going on in Central America and that it must be prepared to withdraw its military presence. That is the one most important ingredient in making the recipe for peace in Central America work.

Mr. Speaker, before I begin my remarks, I would like to make a brief comment. It breaks my heart that Parliament has come to the point that a major statement on Canadian foreign policy contained in the report of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) on his visit to a very troubled region of the world should be made in the presence of-how many Members are present? I suppose the rules do not allow me to comment
Statements by Ministers
on that, but I think it is a sad comment on the state of affairs in Parliament. I will not say any more than that because I do not want to use up any more of the time I am allotted to speak to the Minister's statement.
First I would like to say, on behalf of a great many Canadians, how glad we are that the Secretary of State for External Affairs decided to go to Central America. It was a very important thing for him to do and I hope that what the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) alleged of him is true, and that is that he has been bitten by the bug of Central America and that his level of concern for that area will be heightened as a result of his visit.
I thank him as well for making a statement to the House in spite of the fact that there are so few Members present to hear it. The Minister himself has had something to do with the partial renewal of the practice of making statements in the House. Perhaps some day we will gather together Members of the House in ways that they no longer gather together for these kinds of things.
I was moved, as I always am, by the sincere rhetoric and the analysis of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry, but I am also moved to a rage which I will suppress when I recall the timidity with which the Government to which he belonged dealt with this question in the early days of the Sandinista revolution. At that time, different Canadian policies might have made a difference in the evolution of the situation this Government is now trying to address.
I should begin by saying that I support the major Canadian procedural recommendation made by the Minister in his statement with respect to the formation of a committee. I would hope that the House Leaders would see their way clear to form a special committee with full powers and full flexibility, rather than a subcommittee of some other committee.
I am not sure I agree with the idea of putting a policy before the committee. 1 would like to think about it more before I decide whether or not it is a good idea. Perhaps giving the committee some time, although time is short, to make up its own mind would be a good idea. I am worried that government members of the committee might feel beholden to any policy that would be put before them by the Government, and I would rather have them have an independence of mind at the beginning so that the committee itself could form a view on the situation. However, in order for Canada to be helpful, we will have to take steps in the very short run. Whatever the committee does will have to be done with that in mind.
My problem with the Minister's statement is that, over-all, I find it to be too timid and imbalanced in ways that I hope I will be able to articulate in the time remaining to me. It is timid in its analysis of the superpower relationships in Central America and it is timid about obvious Canadian interests.
I would have thought that when the Secretary of State for External Affairs made a statement on Central America, he would have had some sharp words of protest to register against

December 2, 1987
Statements by Ministers
the attacks on Canadians and Canadian-sponsored projects. I thought that this would be an opportunity for the Canadian Government to send a strong message of disapproval to the American Government about what people supported by that Government are doing to Canadians and Canadian-backed projects.
The Minister said that the peace plan is unanimous and indigenous. These are of course what recommends the plan to everyone. We hope it is respect for those two characteristics of the plan which will cause everyone, including the U.S., to avoid trying to impose their own will on the plan or the region. I am glad the Minister made that statement.
He talks about the need for informed and dispassionate Canadian public opinion about this process. I say to the Minister that the Canadian public is already very well informed on Central America. In fact, I would say the average church-goer in the mainstream churches of this country is probably more informed about Central America than the average Member of Parliament. It is very difficult to walk into the lobby of a United Church, a Roman Catholic Church, an Anglican Church, a Mennonite Church, or various other churches, without finding in front of you an array of literature and material on Central America. So I would just warn the Minister not to be too paternalistic with respect to the Canadian public. There is already a large body of well-informed Canadians who have experience in Central America and have related that experience to other Canadians. On occasion the Minister has chosen to ignore the advice of those Canadians, most recently with respect to the resumption of bilateral aid to Guatemala.
I was glad to hear the Minister referring to pre-1979, say that the then Government of Nicaragua was an oppressive, almost feudal regime which invited revolution. Indeed, that was so, but would it not have been more historically informative, accurate and balanced to have noted that that very regime was put in place and supported by the U.S. for decades? This is part of the problem. It is one thing to say the problem is social and economic, but those problems cannot be divorced from the politics of superpower domination in that area. The fact is that the superpower domination we are talking about when we talk about Central America is American domination going all the way back to the Monroe Doctrine of 1823. It did not originate with Ronald Reagan; it originated in the 19th century and an American commitment to domination of that area of the world.
The Minister displays this imbalance, if you like, in the analysis on page 5 of his statement when he talks about profound skepticism over whether the Sandinistas will let real democracy threaten the revolution which their Constitution describes as irreversible. Why the sarcasm about democracy in Nicaragua and not about elected Governments in other countries of Central America? All the observers of the election in Nicaragua came to the judgment that it was valid. There
are opposition Parties and there is an Assembly. I just think the statement would have been much stronger if he had left out the word "real" and posed a legitimate question about whether the Sandinistas would allow a democratic process to threaten their revolution. That would have been a legitimate question, but to insert this cute adjective of "real" before "democracy" it seems to me, weakened it.

conditions of Central America.
I agree, but did the Nicaraguans or others ask for a model off the shelf? They probably did not, so I think it should be clear that they probably were not in the market for a Cyprus model. It may be that we will not have the six months or eight months that the Minister is talking about to work out that kind of peacekeeping plan. It may be that Canada will have to be part of a much more urgent process. I hope the Minister is at least open to that. I would also like to have seen some mention of how the Minister sees UN involvement. Does he see such involvement in any peacekeeping structure in which Canada would participate? It would have been good to have had that illuminated for the House.
With respect to aid, the Minister says Canada should not abandon its policy of not using aid for political purposes. I agree in the pejorative sense of the word "political", but it is nevertheless a fact that the choice of whom we give aid to and whom we do not is a political act. The resumption of aid to Guatemala was a political act. It will have political effects, even if it did not have ostensible political purposes. That was one of the criticisms made of it. It would send the wrong signal to the Government of Guatemala that perhaps the Canadian Government and people were satisfied with the progress made so far.
I know the Minister has a different view in that he feels this will encourage respect for human rights. However, no matter what side of the argument you are on, there is a political dimension to aid. I hope the Minister is not trying to pretend there is not and that therefore debate about it is illegitimate.
One of the things the Minister could have done in making this announcement was to announce some support for human
December 2, 1987

rights institutions, commissions and the like in Central America. That certainly would have strengthened the perception that human rights are central to the Canadian perception of the problem there.
I want to go back to the analysis, if you like, because this is crucial. The Minister made a good announcement with respect to the committee, but there is an ongoing problem with the analysis. On page 16 he says:
We oppose third party intervention in Central America, whatever the
source, and have made that position clear to both superpowers.
Tie says that as if there were some equivalence to the involvement of the United States and the Soviet Union in Central America. That is like talking about superpower intervention in Afghanistan, as if there were no difference between what the Soviet Union is doing there and the aid that the Americans are giving to the Afghanistan rebels. There is an obvious difference, one that I am sure he would maintain.
That difference exists in Central America. The Contra army, which is basically a proxy army, not a guerrilla army, would disappear minutes after U.S. funding stopped. It is supported by the American Government. It is an extension of long-standing American policy in the area. I just say to the Minister, anyone who knows anything about the situation is not going to accept an analysis which tries to equate the involvement of the two superpowers in the area.
It would be very helpful if just once the Government would condemn outright U.S. funding of the Contras. I can understand the Minister's tactical claim that there may not be that much good to be achieved in persistently haranguing the Americans about their funding of the Contras. I am not sure the tactic works; I am not sure anything works with the U.S. However, if just once, on principle, the Minister or the Government would say that we condemn outright U.S. funding of the Contras and then proceeded from there, that would be so much more helpful. It would clear the air and be helpful to our allies in the U.S. Congress who want to resist the attempts by President Reagan for further funding of the Contras. It is the same tactical debate all over again.
I see the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) is in the House. As a result of being too nice in dealing with President Reagan's policies on acid rain, the Government undermined our real allies in the Congress who wanted to be able to refer to international criticism.
The same mistake is being made with respect to Central America. It would be more helpful if the Minister were able to make a strong statement about Central America, because, whether we like it or not, the U.S. funding of the Contras will have to stop if the peace plan is to succeed. Nicaragua will be unable to meet the standards it has set for itself as long as it is in a permanent state of mobilization. It cannot demobilize until it is no longer under attack, which will not happen until the United States decides to stop funding the Contras.
Statements by Ministers
It is very difficult indeed for the Minister to have an analysis of Central America without addressing that very crucial point.
I return to the imbalance which is finely woven into this analysis. We are told that Radio Catolica was delayed one day in presenting its first news broadcast. One day! There is no mention that this was due to a bureaucratic foul-up with respect to licensing, and that they were able to broadcast on the second day. That should not have been contained in the analysis. There is no mention of all of the opposition newspapers that have been shut down over the years in El Salvador and do not have a hope of ever reopening. Those newspapers were not just censored; the editors were shot, the presses were destroyed and the premises were bombed. Many of those countries do not even bother with censorship, yet acts such as these do not receive the same kind of attention as the shutdown and the reopening of La Prensa, the opposition newspaper in Nicaragua.
The Minister said that there has been no complete amnesty in Nicaragua. The plan does not call for complete amnesty. For instance, the plan does not call for the release of national guardsmen who were prosecuted for crimes committed before the Sandinista revolution. This question of imbalance in the analysis by the Minister is certainly something that I hope the committee could address.
We must be careful in regard to the peace plan. The Arias peace plan is the actual written peace plan. There is also the peace plan as it is perceived by the world through the influence of the United States and the international press. That plan, which does not bear any strict relationship to the actual text, is the one which the United States is interested in fulfilling in Central America. That unofficial plan requires compliance essentially from Nicaragua alone. While this does not mean there will be no benefits to other countries, a double standard applies in this unofficial plan. Nicaragua will have to live up to the letter, the spirit, and the additional interpretation put on it by the United States in this case.
I hope the Canadian Government and this committee can be useful in separating those two plans, between the actual collective judgment of the five central American nations with respect to what was required for peace and that which will come from the White House and the Pentagon about what Nicaragua must do in order for the U.S. to cease the funding of the Contras. That is what is so crucial in the first place, because Nicaragua will not be able to live up to the peace plan as it wishes so long as it is mobilized. No one can expect it to do so. Canada would not be able to live up to those kinds of commitments if we were under attack from an army on a daily basis. We had the War Measures Act over our heads when all that we had was a supposed apprehended insurrection.
We must attempt to avoid the double standard with respect to Nicaragua. I propose that the Government should make a clear statement about the crucial nature of the U.S. role in the funding of the Contras and the need for it to stop. While the Minister's statement today represents progress, such a clear

subtopic: CONSTITUTION ACT, 1867, AND RELATED ACTS MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Ontario Court of Appeal recently acquitted lawyer Harry Kopyto on the offence of scandalizing the court, and a majority of the court found the offence to be in breach of the guarantee of freedom of speech in the Charter of Rights.
The purpose of this Bill is to abolish this archaic offence of scandalizing the court, in addition to conferring upon the Houses of Parliament the right to impose a fine in cases of contempt of Parliament.
The time for abolition of this archaic and repressive offence of scandalizing the court is long overdue. Certainly I want to congratulate Harry Kopyto on having spearheaded this important initiative.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the first time and ordered to be printed.

subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO WHITE PAPER ON TAX REFORM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a petition properly certified which has been signed by residents of the City of Thunder Bay, resident both in my riding of Thunder Bay-Nipigon and in my colleague's riding of Thunder Bay-Atikokan. These persons are protesting the federal Government's White Paper which proposes changes in the taxation structure of Canada. They protest the fact that these proposals do not change an already unfair tax structure which is experienced by average Canadian families but will give wealthy Canadians earning over $100,000 a year, who are presently not paying their fair share, a tax cut.
These proposals will also permit 60,000 profitable corporations to pay no income tax at all and threaten a levy on food and other essential items. The petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to reject these tax changes, to reject the tax on food and to restore full indexation to the personal tax system.
